# Functional Requirements Specification (FRS) Template
## Water Utility SCADA Upgrade

**How to use this template.** Text in `[square brackets]` is a placeholder to replace. Blocks marked **Author guidance** are for the consultant and must be deleted before issue. Numbers in the worked example are illustrative only and must not be copied into a project without engineering review.

---

## 0. Document Control

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Utility / Project | [name] |
| Document no. / Revision | [ ] / [ ] |
| Author / Reviewer / Approver | [ ] |
| Status | Draft / For review / Issued for tender / As-built |

**Author guidance:** Keep a revision log. Every issued revision should list the sections that changed. Tenderers and the utility's operations staff will both read this document, so avoid consultant shorthand.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Purpose and scope
[State what this FRS covers: central SCADA, comms, site PLCs, HMI, historian, and interfaces. State what is excluded, such as the electrical design, civil works, or the treatment plant.]

### 1.2 Intended audience
[Utility operations, IT/OT security, integrator, commissioning team.]

**Author guidance:** Say what this document is *not*. A functional spec says *what the system shall do*, not which product or code structure delivers it. Name specific products only where the utility has a standardisation mandate, and record that reason here.

---

## 2. References and Definitions

### 2.1 Referenced documents
[Utility standards, P&IDs, network diagrams, I/O lists, cyber policy, applicable regulations and standards such as IEC 62443 and IEC 61131-3.]

### 2.2 Definitions and abbreviations
[Define "call", "duty", "standby", "stale", "comms healthy", "local", "remote", "auto", and "manual". Terms like these cause most specification disputes.]

**Author guidance:** Define operating-mode words once here and use them consistently. If "Auto" means something different at a pump station than at a reservoir, say so.

---

## 3. System Overview

### 3.1 Architecture summary
[Diagram plus narrative. Typical baseline: central SCADA with redundant servers, [6] remote booster pump stations, [3] elevated reservoirs, licensed radio primary path, cellular backup path, and one PLC per site.]

### 3.2 Site inventory

| Site ID | Name | Type | PLC | Primary comms | Backup comms | Power backup | Controlled by / Called by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BPS-01 | [ ] | Booster | [ ] | Licensed radio | Cellular | [ ] | Called by RES-[ ] |
| RES-01 | [ ] | Reservoir | [ ] | Licensed radio | Cellular | [ ] | n/a |

### 3.3 Operating philosophy
[Summarise the intended control hierarchy: what is decided centrally, what is decided at the site PLC, and what is decided by the operator.]

**Author guidance:** State the control-authority principle explicitly, for example: *"Each site shall continue to operate safely and maintain supply without the central SCADA. Central SCADA provides supervision, setpoint management, and optional optimisation."* Everything in the later sections depends on this decision, so get the utility to sign off on it early. The site inventory table must show every cross-site dependency, such as which pump station follows which reservoir.

---

## 4. Requirement Conventions

- **ID format:** `FR-[AREA]-[NNN]` (e.g. `FR-CTL-012`). IDs are never reused.
- **Keywords:** *shall* = mandatory; *should* = recommended, deviation needs justification; *may* = optional.
- **Priority:** M (Must) / S (Should) / C (Could).
- **Verification:** T = Test, D = Demonstration, I = Inspection, A = Analysis. Also state the stage: FAT, SAT, or both.
- **Parameters:** Configurable values are written as `{PARAM_NAME}` and listed in the parameter table (Appendix C), with default, range, and owner.

**Author guidance:** Write one testable statement per requirement. If you write "and" or "unless" in a requirement, consider splitting it. Every requirement needs a verification method, and if you cannot say how it would be tested, rewrite it. Never bury numbers in prose. Make them parameters so the utility can tune them without a spec change.

---

## 5. Central SCADA

### 5.1 Server redundancy and failover
[Hot-standby or warm-standby, failover trigger conditions, maximum failover time `{FAILOVER_TIME}`, data continuity during failover, and behaviour on split-brain.]

### 5.2 HMI and operator interface
[Overview screens, site screens, trends, user roles, control-action confirmation, setpoint-change workflow, and screen call-up time.]

### 5.3 Historian and reporting
[Logged tags, sample or deadband rules, retention, backfill from site PLCs after comms outage, standard reports.]

### 5.4 Alarm management
[See Section 11.]

### 5.5 Time synchronisation
[Time source, accuracy, how PLCs are synchronised, and how timestamp source is shown (PLC-stamped vs server-stamped).]

**Author guidance:** Specify *behaviours* (what survives a server failure, what the operator sees) rather than vendor features. Always cover what happens to in-progress operator commands during failover. Decide whether event timestamps come from the PLC or the server, because it matters for post-incident analysis.

---

## 6. Communications

### 6.1 Primary path (licensed radio)
[Polling or report-by-exception, protocol (e.g. DNP3, Modbus), poll cycle `{POLL_CYCLE}`, repeater dependencies, and per-site expected availability.]

### 6.2 Backup path (cellular)
[Activation criteria, switchover time `{COMMS_SWITCH_TIME}`, switch-back criteria and hysteresis, data-use limits, private APN or VPN requirement.]

### 6.3 Comms health determination
[How "comms healthy" is defined at the central end and at each PLC: timeout, missed-poll count, heartbeat. This definition is referenced by later sections.]

### 6.4 Peer-to-peer or relayed data between sites
[State how data from one site reaches another: via central SCADA relay, via direct PLC-to-PLC messaging, or both. State the maximum end-to-end latency `{XSITE_LATENCY}`.]

**Author guidance:** Cross-site control (Section 10) is only as reliable as this section. Be explicit about the path, because a path that relays through the central servers means a server outage affects pump control. Require a heartbeat or quality/age indication on every cross-site value, so a frozen value can be told apart from a steady one. Cellular backup often has higher latency and a different security profile, so check that control strategies still work over it.

---

## 7. Remote Site PLC: General Requirements

### 7.1 Local autonomy
[What each PLC does with no comms.]

### 7.2 Control modes
[Local-Manual, Local-Auto, Remote-Manual, Remote-Auto: definitions, who can change mode, and how mode is displayed.]

### 7.3 Power-up and restart behaviour
[Retained setpoints and modes, restart sequencing, staggered restarts after power failure.]

### 7.4 Instrument fault handling
[Out-of-range detection, rate-of-change checks, fallback on bad analog quality.]

### 7.5 I/O and data
[Reference Appendix A. Define signal quality and timestamp handling.]

**Author guidance:** Write the loss-of-comms behaviour for every site type here or in its own section. A missing "what happens when X fails" is the most common gap in SCADA specifications. State the safe state for each failure explicitly.

---

## 8. Booster Pump Station Functions

### 8.1 Pump control and sequencing
[Duty/standby/assist, alternation rule, minimum run and off times, maximum starts per hour `{MAX_STARTS_PER_HR}`, start sequencing, and soft starter or VFD behaviour.]

### 8.2 Protection and interlocks
[Suction pressure low, discharge pressure high, motor faults, seal or bearing temperature, intrusion, and hardwired vs PLC-implemented trips.]

### 8.3 Station monitoring
[Flow, pressure, run hours, energy, vibration if applicable.]

### 8.4 Call source
[Declare for each station what calls it: local pressure, local wet well, remote reservoir level, operator, or schedule. Cross-reference Section 10.]

**Author guidance:** Keep safety interlocks separate from process control logic, and state which are hardwired. Alternation and starts-per-hour limits protect equipment, so they must win over a call request. Say so explicitly.

---

## 9. Reservoir Site Functions

### 9.1 Level measurement
[Primary and secondary instrument, redundancy, validation logic, units and datum, scaling to a common reference.]

### 9.2 Level alarms and limits
[Low-low, low, high, high-high, overflow. State the setpoints and whether they are PLC or SCADA alarms.]

### 9.3 Inlet/outlet control and valves
[Altitude valves, isolation valves, flow, chlorine residual and other instruments where present.]

### 9.4 Level publication
[Which level value, update rate, and quality flags the reservoir PLC publishes for use by other sites.]

**Author guidance:** Agree on one level datum (percent of range vs metres) for the whole project, since mixing them in cross-site logic invites errors. For elevated reservoirs, specify the effect of wind, inlet turbulence, or filling surges on the signal and require filtering where needed.

---

## 10. Cross-Site Control (Remote-Level-Called Pumps)

### 10.1 Control relationship table

| Pump station | Calling reservoir | Level source | Logic executes in | Data path | Setpoints owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BPS-[ ] | RES-[ ] | [PT-tag] | BPS PLC / Central | [Radio / Cellular / Relay] | [Utility ops] |

### 10.2 Call logic
[Start and stop levels, hysteresis, number of pumps called at each level, minimum run time interaction.]

### 10.3 Data validity and staleness
[Maximum age `{LEVEL_STALE_TIME}`, quality handling, rate-of-change plausibility check.]

### 10.4 Degraded modes
[Behaviour on stale level, on comms loss, on level instrument fault, and on central SCADA loss. Behaviour on recovery.]

### 10.5 Operator override
[Manual call, inhibit, and setpoint change, plus alarms when these are active.]

**Author guidance:** This section needs the most care. For each pump-reservoir pair, decide:
1. **Where the logic runs.** Running it in the pump-station PLC (with the level received directly or relayed) keeps the station independent of the central servers. Running it centrally is simpler to modify but ties pumping to server and comms health.
2. **What the pump does when the level is untrustworthy.** Options include hold last state for a limited time, then fall back to a safe schedule, local pressure control, or stop. The right answer depends on whether the greater risk is reservoir overflow or running dry. Get the utility to choose per pair.
3. **How recovery behaves.** Avoid sudden multi-pump starts when comms return.

Write the worked example below once per relationship, or once as a pattern with a parameter table per pair.

### 10.6 Worked example

> **FR-CTL-012: Booster pump call from remote reservoir level**
> *Priority: M | Verification: T (FAT and SAT) | Applies to: BPS-03, called by RES-02*
>
> **a)** The BPS-03 PLC shall evaluate the pump call logic using the RES-02 level value (`RES02_LVL`, % of range, per the common datum in Section 9.1). Execution shall not depend on the central SCADA servers being available.
>
> **b)** In Remote-Auto, the PLC shall call the duty pump when `RES02_LVL` falls to or below `{BPS03_START_LVL}` (default 45 %) and shall stop it when `RES02_LVL` rises to or above `{BPS03_STOP_LVL}` (default 85 %). The assist pump shall additionally be called at `{BPS03_ASSIST_LVL}` (default 30 %) and stopped at `{BPS03_ASSIST_STOP_LVL}` (default 60 %). Start level shall be lower than stop level by at least `{MIN_DEADBAND}` (default 10 %), and the configuration shall reject entries that violate this.
>
> **c)** The level value shall be considered **valid** only if (i) its quality is Good, (ii) its age is not greater than `{LEVEL_STALE_TIME}` (default 120 s), and (iii) it has not changed faster than `{LEVEL_MAX_RATE}` (default 5 % per minute) between consecutive updates. Otherwise it shall be considered **invalid**.
>
> **d)** On the level becoming invalid, the PLC shall raise a "RES-02 level unavailable at BPS-03" alarm and hold the current pump state (running or stopped) for up to `{HOLD_TIME}` (default 15 min). If the level is still invalid after `{HOLD_TIME}`, the PLC shall [stop the pumps / revert to local discharge-pressure control / follow the fallback schedule in Appendix C. *Author: select one per utility decision.*] and raise a high-priority alarm.
>
> **e)** Pumps shall not be started or stopped in a way that breaches `{MIN_RUN_TIME}`, `{MIN_OFF_TIME}`, or `{MAX_STARTS_PER_HR}`, or any protection interlock in Section 8.2, regardless of the call state. A call that is inhibited for these reasons shall be shown to the operator with the reason.
>
> **f)** When a valid level returns after an invalid period, the PLC shall resume normal call logic only after the value has been valid continuously for `{RECOVERY_CONFIRM_TIME}` (default 30 s). Pump starts on resumption shall be staggered by at least `{START_STAGGER}` (default 10 s).
>
> **g)** Setpoint changes shall be made only by users with the Engineer role, shall be written to the PLC with read-back confirmation, and shall be logged with user, time, old value, and new value. The PLC shall retain setpoints through power loss.
>
> **h)** The operator HMI shall display for BPS-03: the RES-02 level used for control, its age and validity status, the active call state, and any inhibit reason.
>
> **Acceptance test (summary):**
> 1. Vary the simulated RES-02 level through the start and stop points and confirm pump calls at the configured levels with the specified hysteresis.
> 2. Block the level update (radio path disabled) and confirm: alarm at `{LEVEL_STALE_TIME}`, state held for `{HOLD_TIME}`, then the specified fallback.
> 3. Repeat test 2 with radio failed and cellular backup active, and confirm the logic works within cellular latency.
> 4. Disable the central servers and confirm BPS-03 continues call logic unchanged.
> 5. Inject a step change exceeding `{LEVEL_MAX_RATE}` and confirm the value is flagged invalid.
> 6. Restore comms and confirm confirm-time and stagger behaviour.
> 7. Attempt a call during minimum off time and confirm it is inhibited with the reason displayed.

---

## 11. Alarms and Events

### 11.1 Alarm philosophy
[Priority levels, annunciation, acknowledgement, shelving, suppression during planned maintenance, and escalation or callout.]

### 11.2 Alarm list
[Reference Appendix B, which lists tag, description, priority, setpoint, delay, action, and consequence.]

**Author guidance:** Every alarm should require an operator action. Group loss-of-comms alarms so that one radio repeater failure does not generate dozens of alarms. Include system-health alarms, such as server failover, stale data, and cyber events.

---

## 12. Data, Historian, and Reporting

[Retention periods, resolution, data-gap handling after outages, regulatory reports, export formats, and integration with other systems such as GIS, CMMS, or a data lake.]

**Author guidance:** Require that site PLCs buffer data during comms loss and backfill the historian on restoration, and state the minimum buffer duration.

---

## 13. Cybersecurity

[Network zoning, remote access, authentication and role-based access, patching approach, logging, backup and recovery, application whitelisting, and alignment with the utility's policy and IEC 62443.]

**Author guidance:** Cellular backup is the largest added attack surface in this architecture, so specify private APN or VPN, no public IPs, and firewall rules at the site. Reference the utility's cyber policy rather than restating it, and note any regulatory obligations.

---

## 14. Power, Environment, and Physical

[Site power backup duration, UPS and battery monitoring, enclosure rating, temperature range, lightning and surge protection, radio antenna and mast requirements.]

---

## 15. Performance and Capacity

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Data update time to HMI (critical tags) | ≤ [ ] s |
| Server failover time | ≤ `{FAILOVER_TIME}` |
| Radio-to-cellular switchover | ≤ `{COMMS_SWITCH_TIME}` |
| Cross-site level latency | ≤ `{XSITE_LATENCY}` |
| Tag capacity / growth margin | [ ] tags / [ ]% spare |
| System availability | [ ]% |

**Author guidance:** Include spare capacity for future sites and I/O. Base availability figures on what the radio network can actually deliver, and agree how they are measured.

---

## 16. Failure and Degraded-Operation Matrix

| Failure | Central SCADA | Booster station | Reservoir site | Operator indication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One server fails | Standby takes over | No effect | No effect | [ ] |
| Both servers down | Loss of supervision | Continues local/cross-site logic | Continues | [ ] |
| Radio link lost to a site | Cellular used | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] |
| Both links lost to a site | Site shown offline | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] |
| Reservoir level transmitter fails | [ ] | Per Section 10.4 | Alarm | [ ] |
| Site power failure | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] |

**Author guidance:** Complete this matrix with the utility before issue. Each cell should trace to at least one requirement, and gaps found here usually point to missing requirements.

---

## 17. Testing and Acceptance

### 17.1 Factory acceptance test (FAT)
[Simulated sites, failover tests, comms-failure tests.]

### 17.2 Site acceptance test (SAT) and commissioning
[Loop checks, end-to-end tests, cross-site control tests with real comms paths, and reservoir level range checks.]

### 17.3 Availability and reliability trial
[Duration, pass criteria.]

**Author guidance:** Cross-site control must be tested end to end over both radio and cellular paths, not just with simulated values. Reference the traceability matrix (Appendix D) so each requirement maps to a test.

---

## 18. Documentation, Training, and Support

[As-built drawings, configuration backups, operator and maintenance training, spares, warranty, and support response times.]

---

## Appendices

- **A. I/O and tag list template:** Tag, description, site, type (DI/DO/AI/AO), range/units, alarm limits, historian Y/N, source.
- **B. Alarm list template:** Tag, text, priority, limit, delay, action, consequence.
- **C. Parameter table:** `{PARAM}`, description, default, min/max, owner, change authority.
- **D. Requirements traceability matrix:** Requirement ID, source (stakeholder or standard), design reference, test ID, status.
- **E. Open issues and assumptions log:** ID, issue, owner, due date, resolution.

**Author guidance:** Fill Appendices A and C in parallel with the body, since requirements that reference parameters not yet in the table are a common source of late changes.
